title: Growth and Development: Definitions and Principles
body:
## What it is
- **Growth** is the physical, measurable increase in size of the body or its parts. Weight is the best single index of growth. It happens mostly in the first 20 years, fastest in infancy, with a second spurt in adolescence.
- **Development** is the qualitative gain in function, complexity and skill. It can continue after growth stops.
- **Maturation** is the built-in, genetically programmed unfolding of development.
- Growth and development are separate but linked processes.

## Must-know principles
- Continuous from conception to death; always in a set order.
- **Uneven pace**: fast in infancy and adolescence, slower in between.
- **Asynchronous**: body systems grow at different rates. Neurologic tissue peaks in the first year, genital tissue stays small until puberty.
- **Cephalocaudal**: head to tail. A newborn lifts only the head when prone; by about 2 months the chest lifts too.
- **Proximal to distal**: from the midline outward, so shoulder control comes before finger control.
- **Gross to refined**: large-muscle skills come before fine ones (a 3-year-old colors with a fat crayon; a 12-year-old writes with a fine pen).
- There is an optimal time for learning: a child cannot learn a task until the nervous system is mature enough.

## How the exam asks about it
Questions give a behavior and ask whether it is expected for age, or which principle explains it. Rule of thumb: ask which direction the skill travels (head first, center first, big first).

## Related topics
[[Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories]], [[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Maternal and Child Health]]

title: Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories
body:
## Age periods (as given in the handout)
- Neonate: first 28 days. Infant: 1 month to 1 year. Toddler: 1 to 3 years. Preschooler: 4 to 6 years (other parts of the handout say 3 to 5). School-age: 7 to 12 years. Adolescent: 13 to 18 years.

## Freud (psychosexual) vs Erikson (psychosocial)
- Infant: Oral stage; trust vs mistrust (to love and be loved).
- Toddler: Anal stage; autonomy vs shame and doubt (be independent, decide for self).
- Preschool: Phallic stage; initiative vs guilt (start things, problem solving).
- School-age: Latent stage; industry vs inferiority (do things well).
- Adolescent: Genital stage; identity vs role confusion (who am I, adjusting to body image).

## Piaget and Kohlberg in one line each
- Piaget: sensorimotor (infant), preoperational (about 2 to 7), concrete operational (7 to 12), formal operational (12 and up).
- Kohlberg: pre-conventional (toddler/preschool, punishment and reward), conventional (school-age, wanting to be seen as good), post-conventional (adolescent and older, social contract and principles).

## Other facts
- **Maternal bonding** is best started right after birth and can be achieved within the first 30 minutes.
- Vocabulary listed: about 900 words at 3 years, 1500 at 4, 2100 at 5.

## Memory aid
Erikson's words in order: Trust, Autonomy, Initiative, Industry, Identity (made-up aid: "T-A-I-I-I").

## Related topics
[[Growth and Development: Definitions and Principles]], [[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Toddler Development and Toilet Training]], [[Freud's Theory and Defense Mechanisms]]

## Check against your textbook
- Preschool age is given as 3-5 and 4-6 in different places; most texts use 3 to 5 or 6. Check the vocabulary numbers.

title: Infant Development, Fears and Play
body:
## What to know
- Age: birth to 1 year, with very rapid growth and development.
- **Fear**: stranger anxiety. **Play**: solitary. **Toys**: mobiles, rattles, musical toys, crib toys (sensory toys).
- Freud calls this the oral phase: the infant gets pleasure from sucking and mouth stimulation.

## Priority nursing actions
- Meet oral needs: give safe, washable toys and a pacifier.
- **Feed on demand**, following the infant's biologic hunger.
- If oral feeding is not allowed but sucking is, give a pacifier. Why: non-nutritive sucking is a real comfort need.
- Consistent caregivers build trust (Erikson).

## Piaget (sensorimotor, by age)
- 1-4 months: primary circular reactions (own body is the center of attention).
- 4-8 months: secondary circular reactions (interest shifts from body to environment).
- 8-12 months: coordination of secondary reactions.
- 12-18 months: tertiary circular reactions (trial and error).

## Moral development
The handout notes infants learn from parents' approval or scolding; this is a stage before real moral reasoning.

## Related topics
[[Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories]], [[Toddler Development and Toilet Training]], [[Newborn Reflexes]]
outlineRefs: Stages of Growth and Development: Infant

title: Toddler Development and Toilet Training
body:
## What to know
- Age 1 to 3 years; growth alternates between fast and slow bursts.
- **Fear**: separation anxiety. **Play**: parallel (side by side, not together). **Toys**: push-and-pull toys.
- Typical look: pot belly and bow legs. Asks questions constantly. All 20 deciduous teeth are present by about 3 years.
- Freud: anal phase. Erikson: autonomy vs shame. Piaget: preoperational thought begins (symbolic, concrete, literal, egocentric). Kohlberg: pre-conventional, behavior driven by punishment and reward.

## Readiness for toilet training (all must fit the child, not the calendar)
- Stays dry about 2 hours or wakes dry from a nap.
- Can sit, squat and walk; can remove clothing.
- Recognizes the urge to urinate or defecate.
- Wants to please the parent.
- Sits on the toilet 5 to 10 minutes without fussing.

## Negativism
Toddlers say "no" to test independence. Nursing response:
- Offer choices (limited ones).
- Avoid yes/no questions; use open-ended wording.

## Sleep
A consistent bedtime ritual and a security object help.

## Related topics
[[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Preschooler Development and Thinking]], [[Therapeutic Communication]]
outlineRefs: Signs of Readiness for Toilet Training

title: Preschooler Development and Thinking
body:
## What to know
- Age about 3 to 5 years (handout). Grows about 2.5 to 3 inches a year.
- **Fear**: mutilation and castration (fear of body harm, so explain procedures simply and use bandages). **Play**: associative and imitation or make-believe. **Toys**: simple puzzles, dolls, coloring books.
- Around 5 years, mealtime becomes social: manners, conversation, willingness to try new foods.

## Thinking patterns (often tested)
- **Centering**: sees only one feature of an object (a banana is yellow but they miss that it is long).
- **Magical thinking**: animals and objects can think and feel; wishes can cause events.
- **Egocentrism**: own needs and thoughts matter more; cannot see another's view.
- Freud: Oedipus complex (boy attached to mother) and Electra complex (girl attached to father).
- Kohlberg stage 2: acts to satisfy own needs.

## Nursing meaning
Use short, concrete explanations, let the child handle equipment, and reassure that the procedure is not a punishment.

## Related topics
[[Toddler Development and Toilet Training]], [[School-Age Child Development]], [[Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories]]

title: School-Age Child Development
body:
## What to know
- Age about 6 to 12 years; slow, steady growth.
- **Fear**: displacement from school. **Play**: indoor competitive. **Toys**: computer and table games.
- Freud: latent phase. Erikson: industry vs inferiority (wants to do things well).

## Thinking
- **Concrete operations** (Piaget, 7 to 12): systematic reasoning, sorting by color or size, understands **reversibility** (can retrace steps, like a maze backwards).
- Reasoning is **inductive**: specific to general. Example: this plastic toy broke, so all plastic toys break easily.
- Kohlberg conventional level (7-10 years): follows rules to be a good person in own and others' eyes.

## Related topics
[[Preschooler Development and Thinking]], [[Adolescent Development]], [[Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories]]

title: Adolescent Development
body:
## What to know
- Age about 13 to 18; accelerated growth and maturation driven by hormones.
- Growth spurt starts about 1 to 2 years earlier in girls than boys.
- Sebaceous and sweat glands become fully active (acne, body odor).
- **Fear**: displacement from peers. **Play**: outdoor competitive, athletics. 
- Freud: genital phase (new love objects). Erikson: identity vs role confusion.

## Thinking and morals
- **Formal operations** (about 12 and up): hypothetical and scientific reasoning, understands cause and effect, thinks about past, present and future.
- Kohlberg post-conventional: social contract, then universal ethical principles. Many adults never reach the top level.
- Teens see self-care as adult behavior, so they can be responsible for it.

## Nursing tip
"Talk time" is a good activity to sort through attitudes; respect privacy and peer need.

## Related topics
[[School-Age Child Development]], [[Childhood Age Periods and Developmental Theories]], [[Therapeutic Communication]]

title: Apgar Score
body:
## What it is
A quick newborn check done at **1 and 5 minutes**. Five criteria, each scored 0 to 2 (total 10).

## Criteria
- **Appearance** (color): 0 blue, 1 acrocyanosis (blue hands and feet), 2 pink.
- **Pulse**: 0 absent, 1 under 100, 2 over 100.
- **Grimace** (reflex response): 0 none, 1 grimace, 2 vigorous cry.
- **Activity** (muscle tone): 0 limp, 1 minimal flexion, 2 full flexion.
- **Respiration**: 0 absent, 1 weak cry, 2 vigorous cry.

## Interpretation
- 8 to 10: good, healthy.
- 4 to 7: fair; needs observation, stimulation, suctioning.
- 0 to 3 (handout says 1-3): poor; needs immediate resuscitation.

## Exam angle
Heart rate and respiration count most when deciding to act. Airway first (suction, stimulate, keep warm), then breathing, then circulation.

## Memory aid
APGAR itself lists the five criteria (Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration).

## Related topics
[[Newborn Vital Signs and Heat Conservation]], [[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]], [[Newborn Reflexes]]

title: Gestational Age Estimation and Newborn Measurements
body:
## Gestational age signs (premature vs full-term)
- **Skin**: premature is very thin, gelatinous with visible vessels; full-term is thick, leathery or cracked.
- **Lanugo** (fine hair): abundant in premature, thinning later, gone (bald) at full term.
- **Plantar creases**: only at the front in premature; whole sole at full term.
- **Breast**: barely any areola in premature; full areola at term.
- **Ear**: flat and folded in premature; thick and firm at term.
- **Genitals**: male, undescended testes in premature, fully descended at term. Female, prominent labia minora and clitoris in premature; covered by the labia majora at term.

## Measurements
- Normal birth weight 2.5 to 4.0 kg. Doubles at about 6 months, triples at 12 months, quadruples at about 2.5 years.
- **LBW** under 2500 g; **LGA** over 4000 g. Later-born children usually weigh more than the first-born.
- A newborn loses **5 to 10%** of birth weight in the first days because maternal salt and fluid-retaining hormones are gone.
- Length 46 to 54 cm. Head circumference 33 to 35 cm (the largest circumference in an infant). Chest 31 to 33 cm.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Vital Signs and Heat Conservation]], [[Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest]], [[Apgar Score]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's term "term" vs "full-term" columns is confusing (it reads as preterm, near-term, post-term). Confirm the stage each column means.

title: Newborn Reflexes
body:
## Reflexes and when they go
- **Extrusion**: food on the tongue is pushed out.
- **Tonic neck**: head turned to one side, arm and leg on that side extend, the opposite limbs flex. Fades by 3 to 4 months.
- **Palmar grasp**: finger in the palm is gripped. Lessens by 3 to 4 months.
- **Moro (startle)**: loud noise or sudden drop; arms symmetrically abduct and extend. Persisting beyond 6 months may suggest brain damage.
- **Sucking and rooting**: touching lip or cheek makes the baby turn, open the mouth and suck. Rooting usually fades by 3 to 4 months (may last up to 1 year).
- **Stepping (walking)**: held upright with a foot on a surface, baby steps. Present about 3 to 4 months.
- **Babinski**: stroke the sole from heel up the outer side; toes fan out and the big toe dorsiflexes. Disappears after about 1 year. **Absent Babinski** needs a neurologic exam.

## Why it matters
Reflexes show nervous system maturity. A reflex that is absent, asymmetric or persists too long is a red flag. Cerebral palsy often shows persistent primitive reflexes (see [[Cerebral Palsy]]).

## Related topics
[[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest]]

title: Newborn Vital Signs and Heat Conservation
body:
## Normal ranges given in the handout
- Temperature (axillary) about 97.9 to 98 F.
- Apical heart rate 120 to 160 beats/min.
- Respirations 30 to 60 per minute (average 40).
- Blood pressure about 73/55 mm Hg.

## Heat conservation
Newborns save heat by constricting skin vessels (moving blood away from the skin). **Brown fat** in mature newborns makes heat by raising metabolism. Premature infants have less brown fat, so they chill easily.

## Nursing actions (why)
- Dry the baby, cover the head, keep skin-to-skin or under a warmer. Cold stress raises oxygen use and can cause hypoglycemia and breathing trouble.
- Count apical rate for a full minute.

## Related topics
[[Gestational Age Estimation and Newborn Measurements]], [[Apgar Score]], [[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]]

## Check against your textbook
Many texts give axillary temperature as roughly 36.5 to 37.5 C (97.7 to 99.5 F). Verify the temperature and blood pressure numbers.

title: Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest
body:
## Head
- **Anterior fontanel**: soft, flat, diamond-shaped (3-4 cm by 2-3 cm); closes at 12 to 18 months.
- **Posterior fontanel**: triangular, about 0.5-1 cm; closes at 2 to 3 months.
- **Caput succedaneum**: scalp swelling from prolonged labor; **crosses suture lines**; gone in about 3 days.
- **Cephalhematoma**: blood under the periosteum from ruptured capillaries; does **not** cross suture lines (the usual rule; the handout does not say it); absorbs in 3 to 6 weeks.
- **Craniotabes**: localized soft or swollen cranial bone from pressure against the maternal pelvis; corrects itself.

## Eyes
- Permanent color settles between 3 and 12 months. Tear ducts mature by about 3 months. Strabismus is normal until 6 months. Subconjunctival hemorrhage (red spot on sclera) is absorbed in 2 to 3 weeks.

## Ears
- Top of the pinna should line up with the line from inner to outer canthus. **Low-set ears** suggest chromosomal disease (Down syndrome) or kidney anomaly.
- Hearing check: ring a bell about 6 inches from each ear.

## Nose
- Nasal flaring means respiratory distress. Test for choanal atresia by closing the mouth and blocking one nostril at a time; see [[Choanal Atresia]].

## Neck and chest
- Neck is short with skin folds. Rigidity may point to congenital torticollis or meningitis. The thymus is relatively large and triples in size by about 3 years.
- Chest is about 2 inches smaller than the head. **Retractions on inspiration are never normal**; they signal respiratory distress.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]], [[Hydrocephalus]], [[Down Syndrome]]

## Check against your textbook
Cephalhematoma not crossing sutures is added textbook knowledge. The thymus size statement should be verified.

title: Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs
body:
## Abdomen and cord
- Slightly protruding abdomen is normal. A **scaphoid (sunken)** abdomen suggests missing contents (diaphragmatic hernia).
- Bowel sounds should be present within 1 hour of birth.
- Cord: white, gelatinous, **2 arteries and 1 vein**. A **single artery** may mean congenital heart, kidney or chromosomal anomaly. Falls off by day 6 to 10. Taping coins or buttons on an umbilical hernia does not help closure.

## Anus and genitalia
- Check the anus is present and patent. No stool in the first 24 hours: suspect imperforate anus or meconium ileus (see [[Duodenal Atresia and Imperforate Anus]]).
- Male: both testes in the scrotum; absent testes (cryptorchidism) call for a kidney work-up since both arise from similar tissue. Cremasteric reflex may be absent before 10 days. Urethral opening on the tip: dorsal opening is epispadias, ventral is hypospadias (see [[Hypospadias and Epispadias]]).
- Female: swollen vulva from maternal hormones; **pseudomenstruation** (mucus, sometimes blood-tinged) is normal.

## Back and limbs
- Pinpoint opening, dimple or sinus at the spine base suggests spina bifida occulta ([[Spina Bifida]]).
- Very short arms: achondroplasia. **Simian crease**: Down syndrome. Syndactyly (webbing) and polydactyly (extra digits) are noted.
- Hips: should flex and abduct nearly 180 degrees. Locking at 160 to 170 degrees suggests hip subluxation ([[Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip]]).

## Check against your textbook
The handout says the cremasteric reflex tests spinal nerves T8-T10; most texts say L1-L2. Verify.

title: Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn
body:
## Clues and what they suggest
- **Hydramnios** (too much amniotic fluid): congenital GI obstruction (the baby cannot swallow fluid).
- **Oligohydramnios** (too little): genitourinary obstruction or extreme prematurity.
- **Distended abdomen**: ascites, bowel obstruction or tumor. **Empty (sunken) abdomen**: diaphragmatic hernia.
- **Passing a small feeding catheter (no. 8) through the nose**: fails on both sides = choanal atresia; passes the nose but not into the stomach = esophageal atresia.
- **One umbilical artery**: possible urinary or cardiac anomaly or a trisomy.

## How to use
These are screening clues for the nurse to report. They are not diagnoses.

## Related topics
[[Choanal Atresia]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]], [[Newborn Screening]], [[Duodenal Atresia and Imperforate Anus]]

title: Breastfeeding and Bottle-Feeding Safety
body:
## Teaching points
- Almost all drugs pass into breast milk. A breastfeeding mother should check with her provider before taking any medicine.
- Formula: do **not** warm bottles in a microwave; the inside of the milk can get dangerously hot while the bottle feels cool.
- Never prop a bottle: raises the risk of aspiration and otitis media and removes the cuddling infants need.
- Do not put a baby to bed with a bottle: causes **baby bottle caries** (mostly lower teeth per the handout; most texts say upper front teeth).

## Why
Safety teaching rests on aspiration risk, burns and dental decay. 

## Related topics
[[Infant Development, Fears and Play]], [[Maternal and Child Health]], [[Nutrition]]

## Check against your textbook
Bottle caries typically affect the upper front teeth; confirm the handout's "lower teeth".

title: Spina Bifida
body:
## What it is
Incomplete closure of the spinal column (neural tube defect), usually in the 4th week of embryonic life. Exact cause unknown; low maternal **folic acid** is a key factor, plus hereditary and environmental ones.

## Types
- **Occulta**: small dimple or tuft at the lower back; usually no symptoms or treatment.
- **Meningocele**: sac holding meninges and spinal fluid.
- **Myelomeningocele**: sac also holds spinal cord and nerves; the most severe. Associated problems: hydrocephalus, bowel and bladder dysfunction, lower-limb paralysis, meningitis.

## Priority nursing actions
- Protect the sac first: cover with a sterile, moist, non-adherent dressing; use aseptic technique (infection risk to the CNS).
- Position **prone** to reduce tension on the sac.
- Assess neurologic status, head circumference, fontanel fullness and ICP.
- Check the sac for redness, drainage, irritation; give antibiotics as ordered.
- Surgery is done as soon as possible, usually within 24 to 48 hours, to prevent meningeal infection.
- Anticholinergics for urinary continence, laxatives for bowel continence.

## Prevention and screening
- 600 micrograms folic acid daily for pregnant women (first trimester emphasis in handout).
- Raised AFP in maternal serum or amniotic fluid suggests an open spinal lesion. Women with a previous affected child are advised to have testing.

## Related topics
[[Hydrocephalus]], [[Bacterial Meningitis and Encephalitis]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]]

## Check against your textbook
Folic acid timing: textbooks stress taking it before conception and early pregnancy. Latex precautions are often taught for these children but are not in the handout.

title: Hydrocephalus
body:
## What it is
Too much cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the ventricles.
- **Communicating**: impaired absorption in the subarachnoid space.
- **Non-communicating (obstructive)**: flow blocked inside the ventricular system; blockage of the narrow aqueduct of Sylvius is the most common cause.
- Other causes: overproduction by the choroid plexus; risk factors include prior meningitis or encephalitis (adhesions), tumor or hemorrhage, Arnold-Chiari malformation, and meningocele surgery.

## Signs
- Bulging anterior fontanel, widely separated skull bones, "cracked-pot" sound on percussion (**Macewen's sign**), brow bulging (**bossing**), enlarging head circumference.

## Treatment: shunts
- **V-P shunt** (lateral ventricle to peritoneum) is the most used in children. A-V shunt goes to the right atrium. V-U shunt goes to the ureter and needs a nephrectomy.

## Nursing care
- Measure head circumference daily; protect the head; maintain nutrition and fluids.
- Pre-op: small frequent feedings until NPO, reposition the head often and use an egg-crate mattress, prepare family.
- Post-op: vital and neuro signs; lay the child on the **unoperated side** to avoid pressure on the valve; keep flat as prescribed to avoid sudden drainage; if ICP rises, raise the head of bed 15 to 30 degrees; watch for infection and drainage; intake and output.

## Related topics
[[Spina Bifida]], [[Bacterial Meningitis and Encephalitis]], [[Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's HOB elevation advice for rising ICP and "keep flat" order conflict in spirit; follow the surgeon's orders and your textbook.

title: Bacterial Meningitis and Encephalitis
body:
## What it is
- **Meningitis**: inflammation of the membranes around brain and spinal cord. **Encephalitis**: inflammation of the brain itself.
- Bacterial causes: H. influenzae type B, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis; spread by droplets from the nose and throat. Viral causes: mumps, herpes, enteroviruses.

## Assessment
- Fever, irritability, change in consciousness, seizures.
- Stiff neck and **nuchal rigidity**; opisthotonus (arched back).
- **Kernig's sign**: cannot extend the leg when the thigh is flexed at the hip.
- **Brudzinski's sign**: neck flexion makes the hips and knees flex.
- Lumbar puncture: cloudy CSF, raised protein, **low glucose**; smear and culture find the organism.

## Priority nursing actions
1. **Isolate** the infant (first implementation on admission) to stop droplet spread.
2. Airway patent and safe during seizures.
3. Control temperature; neuro checks; watch level of consciousness.
4. Monitor for SIADH (fluid retention, cerebral edema, low sodium).
5. Intake and output, nutrition; identify close contacts for prophylaxis.

## Treatment
IV antibiotics. The handout names penicillin G; real choices depend on age and cultures.

## Related topics
[[Hydrocephalus]], [[Epiglottitis]], [[Sepsis and Septic Shock Recognition]]

## Check against your textbook
Penicillin G as "drug of choice" is oversimplified; broad-spectrum agents are typical until cultures return.

title: Cerebral Palsy
body:
## What it is
A neuromuscular disorder with poor voluntary muscle control, abnormal muscle tone and incoordination. **Anoxia to the brain** is the most significant cause; infection also contributes.

## Types
- **Spastic** (most common): cortex affected; scissor-like gait.
- **Athetoid**: basal ganglia; uncontrolled involuntary movements.
- **Ataxic**: cerebellum; poor balance and coordination.

## Early signs
- Abnormal posturing, feeding difficulty, tremors or seizures, **persistent primitive reflexes**, delayed motor milestones.

## Management
- Passive and active exercise; braces, crutches, walkers.
- Drugs: muscle relaxants, anticonvulsants, tranquilizers.

## Nursing priorities
- Adequate nutrition (feeding takes effort and aspiration is a risk), maximum mobility and self-help skills, safety when walking.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Reflexes]], [[Down Syndrome]], [[Developmental Disorders]]

title: Down Syndrome
body:
## What it is
Trisomy 21: an extra chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes instead of 46). More common with advanced maternal age.

## Features
- Face: wide-set eyes, flat nasal bridge, large tongue. Flat occiput.
- Hands and feet: **simian crease**, plantar furrow, wide gap between first and second toes.
- **Brushfield's spots** (white specks in the iris), low-set ears, potbelly.

## Associated problems
- Intellectual disability, variable from severe to mild.
- Congenital heart defects (VSD), Hirschsprung's disease, leukemia.
- Slow growth with rapid weight gain; delayed or incomplete sexual development.

## Nursing care
- Aim for the child's best developmental potential and coping.
- Plan care by **developmental age**, not chronological age.
- Give consistent care so trust and security can form.

## Related topics
[[Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects]], [[Hirschsprung's Disease]], [[Cerebral Palsy]]

title: Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview
body:
## What it is
Heart or vessel anomalies. **Acyanotic** defects either narrow a vessel or shunt blood **left to right** (oxygenated blood goes back to the lungs), so the child is not blue. Examples: VSD, ASD, PDA, pulmonary stenosis, coarctation of the aorta.

## General signs of heart disease in a child
- Tachycardia, tachypnea, profuse scalp sweating, fatigue, irritability.
- Feeding problems, poor weight gain or failure to thrive, frequent respiratory infections and cough.
- **Murmur** is the most common sign. Hepatomegaly from blood backing up. Sweating on the brow during feeding or crying.

## Complication
**Congestive heart failure** is the most common complication (moist cough, diaphoresis, severe dyspnea).

## Priority nursing thinking
Keep the child calm, small frequent feedings, conserve energy, watch for CHF, give digoxin and diuretics as ordered. Airway and oxygenation come first when the child is in distress.

## Related topics
[[Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects]], [[Patent Ductus Arteriosus and Coarctation of the Aorta]], [[Pulmonary Stenosis]], [[Cyanotic Heart Defects and Tetralogy of Fallot]]
outlineRefs: Signs and Symptoms of heart disorders

title: Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects
body:
## VSD
- Opening between the right and left ventricles; usually a left-to-right shunt. The most common congenital heart defect (about 30%).
- Overloads the right ventricle and lungs. Loud systolic murmur. Can lead to pulmonary hypertension, respiratory failure, and **Eisenmenger syndrome** (shunt reverses right to left).

## ASD
- Opening between the atria: failure of the atrial septum to close.
- Types: ostium primum (low), ostium secundum (center), sinus venosus (near the SVC).
- Small defects: no symptoms. Others: systolic ejection murmur, slow weight gain, right ventricular hypertrophy, tiring, respiratory infections. Heart failure is more likely with ostium primum.

## Treatment and nursing
- Small defects may close on their own.
- Non-surgical: closure device placed in cardiac catheterization. Surgical: open repair on bypass, ideally before school age.
- Teach the family about treatment options; monitor for CHF.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview]], [[Down Syndrome]], [[Patent Ductus Arteriosus and Coarctation of the Aorta]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout says ASD defects are repaired mainly in girls because of pregnancy-related pulmonary hypertension. This is unusual; verify the indication. It also describes ASD as more oxygenated blood going right, which is the left-to-right shunt.

title: Patent Ductus Arteriosus and Coarctation of the Aorta
body:
## PDA
- The fetal ductus arteriosus fails to close after birth. Blood flows from the aorta back to the pulmonary artery, raising left ventricular work and lung congestion.
- Signs: loud **machinery-like murmur**, repeated respiratory infections, CHF (poor feeding, fatigue, tachypnea), poor weight gain, widening pulse pressure.
- Treatment: **ibuprofen or indomethacin** (prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors) can close it in premature infants. Otherwise close during catheterization or by surgery. Some close on their own.

## Coarctation of the aorta
- Narrowing of the aorta near the ductus.
- High blood pressure in the **arms** with headache, dizziness, nosebleeds; **weak or absent femoral pulses** (bounding radial pulse); leg cramps; systolic murmur.
- Treatment: digoxin and diuretics for CHF, balloon angioplasty, or surgical removal of the narrow part with end-to-end joining.

## Nursing focus
Compare arm and leg pulses and blood pressure; monitor for CHF.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview]], [[Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects]], [[Pulmonary Stenosis]]

title: Pulmonary Stenosis
body:
## What it is
Narrowing at the entrance of the pulmonary artery. The right ventricle works harder, hypertrophies, and less blood reaches the lungs. **Pulmonary atresia** is the extreme form: no blood to the lungs.

## Assessment
- Characteristic murmur; may be symptom-free.
- Severe narrowing: cyanotic newborn, CHF, signs of low cardiac output.

## Treatment
- Non-surgical: dilate the valve during cardiac catheterization.
- Surgical: closed valvotomy in infants; pulmonary valvotomy on bypass in older children.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview]], [[Cyanotic Heart Defects and Tetralogy of Fallot]], [[Patent Ductus Arteriosus and Coarctation of the Aorta]]

title: Cyanotic Heart Defects and Tetralogy of Fallot
body:
## Cyanotic defects
Blue blood (right to left) mixes into the body's supply. Examples: tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, tricuspid atresia, transposition of the great vessels.
- Signs: **central cyanosis**, clubbing, fatigue, poor growth, recurrent respiratory infection, squatting in older children, high hematocrit.
- Complications: clots and brain infarcts, heart failure.

## Tetralogy of Fallot (4 features)
- Pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta, VSD.
- Cyanosis at birth or in the first year, exertional dyspnea, slow weight gain.
- **Tet spell**: irritability, pallor, blackouts or convulsions.

## Priority actions in a tet spell
- Place the child in the **knee-chest** position (infants: side-lying with knees up; older children squat). Why: it raises systemic resistance and brings more blood to the lungs. Then oxygen, keep calm, warm, and give drugs as ordered.
- Promote rest, prevent infection, give digitalis/diuretics when ordered.

## Tricuspid atresia
- Tricuspid valve is closed; no flow from right atrium to right ventricle. Survival depends on a patent foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus.
- Cyanosis, tachycardia, dyspnea; older children have clubbing.
- **IV PGE1** keeps the ductus open. Surgery: vena cava-to-pulmonary shunt or Fontan-type procedure.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Heart Defects: Acyanotic Overview]], [[Pulmonary Stenosis]], [[Ventricular and Atrial Septal Defects]]
outlineRefs: Two Broad Classifications: Cyanotic Heart Defects

title: Choanal Atresia
body:
## What it is
Blockage at the back of the nasal passage (choana), one or both sides. Newborns breathe through the nose, so bilateral atresia is an airway emergency.

## Danger sign
**Cyanosis during feeding** that improves with crying (the open mouth lets the baby breathe).

## Priority actions
- Airway first: insert an **oral airway** to relieve breathing trouble temporarily.
- Surgery perforates the atresia and may leave a stent or need repeated dilation.
- Maintain oral airway patency, monitor breathing, pre and post-op care, early screening (a catheter will not pass through the nose).

## Related topics
[[Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn]], [[Airway Management in the Primary Survey]], [[Newborn Assessment: Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Neck and Chest]]

title: Tonsillitis, Adenoiditis and Tonsillectomy Care
body:
## What it is
Inflammation of lymphoid tissue in Waldeyer's ring. The usual cause is group A beta-hemolytic strep. Swollen tissue can obstruct breathing and swallowing; sore throat, altered smell, taste and hearing. Labs: leukocytosis, raised ESR.

## Why it matters
- Untreated strep can cause **acute glomerulonephritis** (5 to 21 days later) and **rheumatic fever** (2 to 6 weeks later), whose worst outcome is rheumatic heart disease, mainly the mitral valve.

## Surgery
- Antibiotics for the acute illness. Removal after 2 to 3 weeks if recurrent documented strep (handout: 4 per year) with swallowing and speech problems.
- Avoid surgery in children under about 5-6 years unless life-threatening, with bleeding disorders, or during acute respiratory infection.

## Post-op priorities (airway and bleeding first)
- Position **prone or side-lying** to drain secretions.
- Suction ready but do not suction unless obstructed.
- **Frequent swallowing = possible hemorrhage**. If bleeding, turn to the side and notify the doctor.
- Discourage coughing and throat clearing.
- Give clear, cool, non-citrus, non-carbonated fluids; avoid milk (coats the throat) and red liquids (look like blood).
- No straws, forks or sharp objects. Acetaminophen for pain.
- Teach: report bleeding, earache, fever; stay away from crowds until healed.

## Related topics
[[Epiglottitis]], [[Airway Management in the Primary Survey]]

title: Epiglottitis
body:
## What it is
Life-threatening inflammation of the epiglottis, classically by H. influenzae; a **medical emergency**.

## Assessment
- Sudden severe inspiratory stridor and hoarseness.
- Drooling and difficulty swallowing.
- Fever; high white count.
- **Tripod position**: leaning forward with chin thrust out and mouth open.

## Priority actions
1. Protect the airway: keep the child calm, do not leave unattended; prepare for intubation or tracheostomy.
2. **Never** examine the throat with a tongue blade or take a throat culture. Gagging can cause complete airway closure.
3. Give humidified oxygen and IV antibiotics (a third-generation cephalosporin).
4. Swelling usually decreases after about 24 hours; extubation around day 3 (handout).

## How the exam asks about it
A drooling, upright, anxious child: do NOT inspect the throat; call for help and prepare airway equipment.

## Related topics
[[Airway Management in the Primary Survey]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]], [[Tonsillitis, Adenoiditis and Tonsillectomy Care]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout says "children need moist air"; current practice focuses on securing the airway and avoiding upsetting the child.

title: Pediatric Bronchial Asthma and Status Asthmaticus
body:
## What it is
A chronic, **reversible** narrowing of the bronchi from allergens (extrinsic) or other triggers (intrinsic), causing bronchospasm and swelling.

## Signs
- Wheezing, **worse on expiration**; rapid labored breathing; dry hacking cough that becomes rattling with frothy clear sputum.

## Status asthmaticus
Distress that does not respond to vigorous treatment; can end in respiratory failure and death, so it is an emergency.

## Priority nursing actions
- **Upright position**; prepare for ventilation.
- Monitor vital signs, breath sounds, retractions, ABGs and oxygen saturation.
- Give oxygen, IV fluids and emergency drugs as ordered.
- Medications by nebulizer or metered-dose inhaler; use nebulizer if the child cannot use the MDI.
- Chest physiotherapy (clapping, vibration, postural drainage) is **not** for an acute attack.

## Drugs mentioned
- Albuterol (bronchodilator), cromolyn (preventive), inhaled corticosteroids. 

## Related topics
[[Respiratory Failure Recognition]], [[Breathing Assessment in the Primary Survey]], [[Epiglottitis]]

## Check against your textbook
The mild/moderate/severe drug scheme in the handout is simplified. Verify steps and dosing intervals using current guidelines.

title: Cleft Lip and Cleft Palate
body:
## What it is
Failure of tissues to fuse in embryo. Causes: heredity, radiation, rubella, chromosomal abnormalities, teratogens. Lip cleft ranges from a notch to complete separation to the nose; palate cleft affects the uvula, soft and hard palate.

## Pre-op feeding care
- Assess suck, swallow, secretions and breathing; monitor weight and intake.
- Enlarge the nipple, stimulate sucking, rest during feeding.
- Hold **upright**; direct formula to the **side and back** of the mouth.
- Position on the side after feeding; keep suction and a bulb syringe at the bedside. Encourage breastfeeding if possible.

## Surgery timing
- **Cheiloplasty** (lip) in the first weeks of life, before the palate.
- **Palatoplasty** (palate) between 12 and 18 months, before faulty speech develops.

## Post-op lip
- Lip protector taped to cheeks; lie on the back or side opposite the repair, **not prone**.
- Clean the suture line with normal saline after feeding.
- Prevent crying; keep the Logan bar dry.

## Post-op palate
- May lie prone. Feed by bottle, breast or cup.
- **No** tooth brushing, hard foods, oral suction, sharp objects or objects in the mouth. Soft elbow restraints may be used. Give analgesics.

## Related topics
[[Choanal Atresia]], [[Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn]], [[Pyloric Stenosis]]

## Check against your textbook
Many sources place lip repair at about 2 to 3 months rather than the first weeks.

title: Pyloric Stenosis
body:
## What it is
Overgrowth of the pyloric circular muscle narrows the passage from stomach to duodenum. Starts in the first weeks of life.

## Assessment
- At about 4 to 6 weeks, vomiting soon after feeds that becomes **projectile and non-bilious** (the block is before the bile duct).
- Visible peristaltic waves moving left to right across the upper abdomen.
- **Olive-shaped mass** in the epigastrium, right of the navel.
- Hungry, irritable infant; dehydration, malnutrition, electrolyte imbalance.

## Treatment and nursing
- **Pyloromyotomy** (incision of the pyloric muscle, can be laparoscopic).
- Before surgery: monitor vital signs, intake and output, weight, hydration and electrolytes; withhold oral feeds; give IV fluids.
- Offer a pacifier for non-nutritive sucking.

## Related topics
[[Duodenal Atresia and Imperforate Anus]], [[Hirschsprung's Disease]], [[Lactose Intolerance]]

title: Lactose Intolerance
body:
## What it is
Lack of lactase enzyme in the small intestine, so lactose is not digested.

## Assessment
After milk products: abdominal distention, cramping, colic, diarrhea and gas.

## Nursing teaching
- Remove the offending dairy; soy-based formula for infants.
- Lactase enzyme tablets can help.
- Give calcium and vitamin D to prevent deficiency.
- Limit milk to one glass at a time and take it with other foods.
- Hard cheese, cottage cheese and yogurt are often tolerated; small daily amounts may help gut bacteria adapt.
- Teach hidden lactose sources.

## Related topics
[[Celiac Disease]], [[Nutrition]], [[Pyloric Stenosis]]

title: Celiac Disease
body:
## What it is
Intolerance to **gluten**, a protein in barley, rye, oats and wheat (mnemonic B-R-O-W). It damages the intestinal lining, shrinks the villi, and blocks nutrient absorption. Symptoms appear about 3 to 6 months after gluten is started.

## Assessment
- Diarrhea (acute or slowly developing), **steatorrhea** (fatty stool), anorexia, abdominal pain and bloating, vomiting, muscle wasting especially in the buttocks and limbs.

## Celiac crisis
Triggered by infection, fasting or gluten: profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting, rapid dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, acidosis. This is the emergency to prioritize (fluids and electrolytes).

## Nursing care
- **Lifelong gluten-free diet**; use corn, rice and millet.
- Allowed: meat, fish, eggs, milk, vegetables, fruits, rice, corn products.
- Avoid: breads, cereals, pasta, crackers, cookies, beer, malted milk, prepared puddings, commercial ice cream.
- Supplement iron, folic acid and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

## Related topics
[[Lactose Intolerance]], [[Nutrition]], [[Hirschsprung's Disease]]

## Check against your textbook
Oats are debated as to gluten content. The handout's "toxic glutamine" explanation is an older idea.

title: Duodenal Atresia and Imperforate Anus
body:
## Duodenal atresia
- Part of the duodenum is missing or closed.
- **Early bilious vomiting**, no abdominal distention, vomiting continues even when not fed, few meconium stools then none.
- X-ray: **double bubble** sign (two air-filled spaces).
- Often linked to hydramnios and Down syndrome (added knowledge).

## Imperforate anus
- No meconium passed; anal canal absent or narrowed.
- Absent "wink" reflex around the anus; cannot insert a rubber catheter into the rectum.
- Abdominal distention develops.
- Repair depends on severity; a fistula to the bladder or vagina makes it harder.

## Nursing
- Check anal patency on the first newborn exam; report no stool in 24 hours; keep NPO and prepare for surgery.

## Related topics
[[Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn]], [[Hirschsprung's Disease]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]]

## Check against your textbook
Added: Down syndrome link with duodenal atresia. Surgery type is not described in the handout for duodenal atresia.

title: Hirschsprung's Disease
body:
## What it is
Absent nerve ganglion cells in part of the bowel (usually rectum), so that segment cannot move stool; the colon above enlarges (aganglionic megacolon).

## Assessment
- No meconium in the first 48 hours; symptoms within the first weeks.
- Abdominal bloating, bile-stained vomit, **ribbon-like** stools or small watery stools, fecal-smelling breath.
- Poor appetite, delayed growth, anemia.
- Diagnosis: abdominal X-ray, barium enema, rectal biopsy.

## Treatment
Surgical bowel resection / pull-through (around one year) and temporary colostomy.

## Post-op nursing
- Measure abdominal girth daily; check the incision and the stoma (red and moist is healthy).
- NPO until bowel sounds or flatus return (48-72 h); NG tube to intermittent suction; IV fluids, then advance diet.
- Teach colostomy and skin care.

## Related topics
[[Down Syndrome]], [[Duodenal Atresia and Imperforate Anus]], [[Celiac Disease]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout says low-fiber, high-calorie, high-protein diet; verify. Pre-op irrigations with saline are mentioned.

title: Abdominal Wall Defects: Omphalocele, Gastroschisis and Umbilical Hernia
body:
## Omphalocele
Bowel or organs protrude through the umbilical ring **inside a translucent sac**. Cover the sac right after birth with sterile gauze soaked in warm saline to prevent drying.

## Gastroschisis
Bowel protrudes **lateral to the umbilical ring with no covering membrane**. Cover loosely with saline-soaked pads and wrap in plastic drape; surgery within hours. The handout says position supine and keep the bowel moist.

## Umbilical hernia
Small muscle defect lets peritoneum bulge at the navel, more obvious with crying. Usually closes by age 3 without treatment. Repair indications: strangulation, no closure by age 4-5, very large defect under 2, or cosmetic. Coins or binders do not help.

## Priority
Protect exposed tissue from infection, drying and heat loss before surgery.

## Related topics
[[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]], [[Inguinal Hernia and Hydrocele]], [[Congenital Anomaly Appraisal in the Newborn]]

## Check against your textbook
Gastroschisis positioning is often side-lying to protect bowel blood supply; verify.

title: Talipes (Clubfoot)
body:
## What it is
Foot deformity, more common in boys, likely polygenic, usually one foot.
Four types: plantar flexion (equinus), dorsiflexion, varus (turned in), valgus (turned out).

## Management
- Start in the newborn period: manipulation and stretching, then casts placing the foot in overcorrection.
- Casts changed every 1 to 2 weeks because infants grow fast; final cast removed after about 6 weeks.
- Denis Browne splints maintain correction; surgery (posteromedial release) when needed.
- Parents then do passive range-of-motion exercises several times a day for months.

## Nursing
Check circulation, skin and cast edges; teach cast care and exercises.

## Related topics
[[Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]]

title: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
body:
## What it is
A shallow or flat acetabulum, so the femoral head does not sit in the socket. Causes: genetics and maternal hormones, mechanical factors like **breech** position, newborn ligament laxity.

## Assessment
- **Barlow test**: pushes the hip backward; slipping out is positive (unstable).
- **Ortolani maneuver**: reduces a dislocated hip; a palpable "clunk" as it goes back in. 
- Uneven leg creases, a **Galeazzi sign** (one knee lower), limited abduction.

## Management
- Hip held **flexed and abducted** to deepen the socket: multiple diapers, splints, casts. A few need surgery with a pin.
- Early detection is best.

## Nursing
Teach parents how to apply and care for the device; skin checks; do not narrow the diapering position.

## Related topics
[[Talipes (Clubfoot)]], [[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's Barlow/Ortolani wording is jumbled. Pavlik harness, the standard device, is not named.

title: Hypospadias and Epispadias
body:
## What it is
- **Hypospadias**: urethral opening on the underside (ventral) of the penis.
- **Epispadias**: opening on the top (dorsal) surface.
- Chordee: downward curve of the penis.

## Signs
Misplaced meatus; difficulty making a straight urine stream.

## Management
- Minor cases with the opening on the glans need no treatment.
- Severe cases: surgical repair, ideally around age 2 to 3 or before school (and before toilet training concerns).

## Nursing
- Careful newborn genital exam; teach family.
- Do **not** circumcise before evaluation, as the foreskin may be needed for repair (added knowledge).

## Related topics
[[Newborn Assessment: Abdomen, Cord, Genitalia, Back and Limbs]], [[Inguinal Hernia and Hydrocele]]

## Check against your textbook
Repair timing is usually earlier (6 to 18 months) in current practice; the circumcision advice is added knowledge.

title: Inguinal Hernia and Hydrocele
body:
## Inguinal hernia
Incomplete closure of the processus vaginalis lets bowel descend toward the scrotum.

## Hydrocele
Fluid in the scrotal sac.
- **Non-communicating**: seen at birth; leftover peritoneal fluid trapped; needs no treatment.
- **Communicating**: processus vaginalis stays open to the abdomen; goes with a hernia.

## Nursing thinking
Report a firm, painful scrotal mass or vomiting with a bulge (possible strangulation).

## Related topics
[[Hypospadias and Epispadias]], [[Abdominal Wall Defects: Omphalocele, Gastroschisis and Umbilical Hernia]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout does not give hernia treatment (surgical repair) or strangulation signs; these are added.
